adds.title: Elazığ Cumhuriyet Meydanı'nda LGBTİ+ düşmanı miting (Kaos GL)
adds.summary: On 19 December 2022 an anti-LGBT hate rally was held at Elazığ's Cumhuriyet (Republic) Square under a banner reading "LGBT sapkınlıktır" ("LGBT is perversion"), and ruling AKP deputy mayor Nazif Bilginoğlu took part. The rally statement denounced consensual same-sex relationships and "homosexual marriage" as a "revolting loss of reason" in Western states, used hostile terms such as "perverse" and "degenerate mentality", and linked gender/sexual themes to Turkey's denunciation of the Istanbul Convention. It documents state-facilitated, locally active anti-LGBT mobilization in this particular province, relevant to the hostility a visibly LGBTQ traveler could face in Elazığ.

adds.title: LGBT rights in Turkey (Wikipedia)
adds.summary: National-framework page for the law Elazığ province (like every Turkish province) stands under. Homosexuality has been decriminalised since 1858 and gender-reassignment surgery is legal since 1988, and discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited; but same-sex relationships, marriage, civil unions and same-sex adoption receive no legal recognition, and LGBTI people are barred from serving openly in the military. Since 2015 the authorities have repeatedly banned and forcibly dispersed Pride marches using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions. In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49, ahead only of Azerbaijan and Russia; in early 2026 the government was reported to be considering criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex and general morality".

adds.title: Turkey: 19 LGBTI Pride marchers must be acquitted in forthcoming trial (ILGA-Europe)
adds.summary: ILGA-Europe press release (7 December 2020) urging Turkish courts to acquit 19 human rights defenders prosecuted for taking part in a peaceful Pride march at Middle East Technical University (METU) in Ankara in May 2019. It documents that even a campus Pride march can draw criminal prosecution in Turkey and calls on the state to uphold its domestic and international commitments and dismiss all charges. It reflects the national freedom-of-assembly climate and legal exposure of LGBT advocacy that a visitor in Erzincan province would be judged against under the same national framework.
